analysis.one_liner: Gives every child a federally managed $1,000 savings account funded by higher taxes on large estates and investment gains.
analysis.headline: Booker's plan to give every U.S. child a $1,000 savings account paid for by higher estate and capital gains taxes was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single action before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a government-run savings account for every American child: $1,000 at birth, then yearly deposits of up to $2,000 for lower-income families, phasing out above five times the poverty line. The money would grow in a fund invested like federal employees' retirement savings and could be spent starting at age 18 only on education, a home, or retirement savings. To pay for it, the bill raises the estate tax to as high as 65% on the largest fortunes, restores the $3.5 million estate exemption, ends the tax break on inherited investment gains above $100,000, and raises the capital gains rate from 20% to 24.2%.
analysis.who_benefits: American children, with the largest deposits going to children in families below 500% of the poverty line: $1,000 at birth plus up to $2,000 a year, so a child in a family at or below the poverty line could have roughly $37,000 in deposits before investment growth by age 18. Accounts would not count against eligibility for federal benefits like student aid, and money could be withdrawn for college tuition, a first home, or savings after age 59½. Higher education institutions and the housing market would also see new demand from account withdrawals.
analysis.who_benefits_short: American children, especially in low-income families

how_it_helps.text: Every child born after 2019 would get a $1,000 federally funded account at birth, and families below 500% of the poverty line would receive annual deposits on a sliding scale starting at $2,000 a year for the poorest households.

The money could be withdrawn at 18 only for qualified wealth-building uses — education, buying a home, or savings after 59½ — and account balances would be ignored when determining eligibility for any federally funded benefit, including student financial aid, so savings would never cost a family benefits.

Accounts would be held in a single government fund managed with the same fiduciary rules as the federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan, invested in 30-year U.S. Treasury bonds, with independent audits and annual statements to account holders — no fees to private money managers.

The program would be paid for by households at the top: the estate tax rate would rise from 40% to 45% (65% above $50 million), the estate exemption would drop back to $3.5 million, inherited and gifted capital gains would be taxed at death above a $100,000 exclusion ($1 million for qualified farm property), and the top capital gains rate would rise from 20% to 24.2%.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthiest households: large estates (the tax rate would rise to 45%, and to 65% on amounts over $50 million, with the exemption cut to $3.5 million), and anyone realizing capital gains, which would be taxed at 24.2% at the top rate and for the first time taxed when assets are passed by gift or at death, beyond a $100,000 exclusion. Executors and heirs could spread death-related capital gains tax over up to 15 years, and farm real property gets a $1 million exclusion and a higher special-use valuation, softening the impact on family farms.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large estates and wealthy asset holders

drawbacks.text: The bill is a very large new entitlement: deposits of up to $2,000 per child per year flow to families well up the income scale (up to 500% of the poverty line, roughly $105,000 for a family of three at the time), and the bill does not cap the total number of accounts or state the program's total cost.

Account money could only be invested in 30-year U.S. Treasury bonds, which are safe but historically return less than a diversified stock portfolio over an 18-year horizon, so children's balances would likely grow more slowly than in a typical 529 college plan.

The money is locked up: no withdrawals before age 18 except for college, and after 18 only for education, a home purchase, or savings past 59½ — a family facing an emergency before the child turns 18 gets nothing from the account.

Taxing capital gains at death falls on heirs of any appreciated asset beyond the $100,000 exclusion — a family business or rental property could trigger a large tax bill, even with the 15-year installment option; the bill responds with special carve-outs for farm property, which adds complexity and recapture rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: a guaranteed asset of tens of thousands of dollars for poor children at no benefit-cliff cost, financed entirely by taxes that fall almost exclusively on the richest estates and investment income. The costs are the bill's design trade-offs — it is expensive, it spreads deposits well into the middle class, it locks money into low-return Treasury bonds, and the capital-gains-at-death change would create real paperwork and potential liquidity strain for heirs of businesses and farms, which the bill patches with farm-specific carve-outs. On balance it is a straightforward wealth transfer from concentrated inheritances to children's savings, but the deposit schedule and investment restrictions are blunter and costlier than a strictly poverty-targeted design would be.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the American Opportunity Accounts Act on July 23, 2019.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance that same day; it was never reported out.
Only one other senator, a Democrat, signed on as a cosponsor over the entire Congress.
The action history shows no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Holders of large estates and appreciated assets are better off, because the estate tax increase, the 65% surtax, and the taxation of capital gains at death never took effect; no child received an account.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large estates and holders of appreciated assets

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its only Senate sponsor; it was read twice and referred to the Finance Committee.

for.name: One Democratic cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: Charles Grassley
against.what_they_did: The bill was referred to his committee on July 23, 2019, and the committee took no action on it — no hearing or markup — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it never left committee, so it was never eligible for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call record exists; the bill had one Democratic sponsor and one Democratic cosponsor and died in a Republican-chaired committee without any Republican support.

industries.note: The bill's funding comes straight from them: a 45% estate tax (65% above $50 million), the $3.5 million exemption restored, capital gains taxed at death beyond $100,000, and a 24.2% top capital gains rate. Their tax bill is the program's funding source, so their interest runs directly against the children the bill would serve.

The bill shuts down major estate-tax avoidance techniques — short-term grantor retained annuity trusts, grantor-trust games, and heavily discounted valuations of farm and business property — which are the core of high-end estate-planning work. Less loophole planning means less fee income.

industries.industry: Private asset managers and financial services firms
industries.note: The bill routes children's savings through a single government fund invested only in Treasury bonds and managed like the federal employees' Thrift Savings Plan, leaving no role or fee stream for private fund managers, brokerages, or 529-plan administrators. A large new pool of household wealth would stay outside the private fee economy.
Account withdrawals for qualified tuition and related expenses are explicitly allowed before age 18, creating a new dedicated source of tuition payment for a generation of students.

The bill raises the special-use valuation cap for farm real property from $750,000 to $3 million and gives qualified farm property a $1 million capital gains exclusion at death, but heirs who sell or stop farming within 10 years must repay the benefit.
